title: A Few Good Men from Univac
author: David E. Lundstrom
note: Selected: IEEE-USA's 1988 literary award explicitly recognized this book; Bernard Galler and computer historians Paul Ceruzzi and David Mindell also praised it. Reader response is positive but only 23 ratings, so broad-reader consensus is not claimed. An engineering memoir about computer design, commercial constraints and organizational failure, not technical training. US setting does not make the globally consequential computing mechanisms a predominantly American social-history topic; T11=0. Technology development is central, T12=0. V3's technology memoir exception also applies. No serious veto established; insider selection and contemporary myth-making limit reliability.
notes: First-hand engineering experience is corroborated by specialist attention, but memoir selection and company loyalties limit neutrality.
Connects computer design, manufacturing, airline systems, corporate organization and competition.
Strong transferable lessons about technical autonomy, project failure and bureaucracy.
Explains practical constraints behind design and organizational choices; not merely a sequence of personalities.

D=8, moderate confidence from Galler's assessment, Ceruzzi and Mindell review excerpts, Walker's detailed review and reader reports. Different project failures add constraints; anecdotes have educational value, though no full-text audit was performed.
Development and organization lessons remain durable despite obsolete machines.
Direct fit for computing, engineering and industrial organization.
Participant with an IEEE literary award and serious historian attention; not a comprehensive archival history.
Lively engineering stories are connected through the author's career.
Concrete practitioner language, with retrospective judgments requiring context.
